issues.legal_issue: An appeal to the Supreme Court is maintainable from the operative decree finally determining the parties’ rights when that decree was passed after the Constitution came into force and the constitutional appeal requirements are satisfied.
material_facts: The Rajasthan High Court’s review judgment modified the decree and was the operative decree finally determining the parties’ rights.
That decree was passed after the Constitution came into force, and the appeal requirements under Article 133 were found to be satisfied.
The respondent argued that the earlier decision of the former Jaipur High Court had become final under the Jaipur State Code of Civil Procedure.
issues.conclusion: The appeal was competent; the earlier Jaipur State procedural code did not determine the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction over the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The operative decree that finally and conclusively determines the parties’ rights governs appealability. When that decree is passed after the Constitution comes into force, Article 133 applies if its requirements are fulfilled; a former State’s procedural code cannot determine the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction.

predicates.civil_appeal_to_supreme_court: A party brings a civil appeal to the Supreme Court.
predicates.operative_final_decree_after_constitutio: The decree finally determining the parties’ rights was passed after the Constitution came into force.
predicates.constitutional_appeal_requirements_satis: The requirements for an appeal under the Constitution are fulfilled.

issues.definition: When a civil appeal to the Supreme Court challenges an operative final decree passed after the Constitution came into force and the constitutional appeal requirements are satisfied, the appeal is maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: A certificate for appeal is justified when the property-value requirement is met and the case involves a substantial question of law.
material_facts: An inquiry reported that the value of the property, or the value of the property affected by the decision, exceeded the required threshold.

The case involved the substantial question whether a testamentary disposition in favour of a female heir gave her only a limited estate absent evidence of an intention to give her an absolute interest.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in granting the certificate for appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The requirements of Article 133 were met where the property-value requirement was satisfied and a substantial question of law was involved.

predicates.civil_appeal_certificate_proceeding: A party seeks a certificate to bring a civil appeal to the Supreme Court.
predicates.property_value_requirement_met: The value of the property, or of the property affected by the decision, meets the applicable threshold.
predicates.substantial_question_of_law_involved: The case presents a substantial question of law.

issues.definition: In a civil appeal certificate proceeding, a certificate is justified when the property-value requirement is met and the case involves a substantial question of law.

issues.legal_issue: Possession is presumed to continue until dispossession, so a possession suit is within limitation when the claimant’s possession continued until the defendant dispossessed the claimant within the applicable limitation period.
material_facts: The courts below found that the plaintiff had been in possession during the lifetime of the female donee and continued in possession afterward.
Even if the tenant left the house and the plaintiff did not lock it, there was no established earlier dispossession; the defendant later entered into possession.
The suit was filed within twelve years of the defendant’s entry into possession.
issues.conclusion: The suit was within limitation, and there was no valid ground to disturb the concurrent finding on possession.
issues.legal_principle: The law presumes continuity of possession. If a person’s possession is established, it is presumed to continue until that person is dispossessed.

rule.if: civil_possession_suit and claimant_possession_established and no_earlier_dispossession_proved and suit_filed_within_limitation_period_after_dispossession

predicates.civil_possession_suit: A claimant brings a civil suit seeking possession of property.
predicates.claimant_possession_established: The claimant’s possession of the property is established.
predicates.no_earlier_dispossession_proved: No dispossession of the claimant before the defendant’s entry is proved.
predicates.suit_filed_within_limitation_period_afte: The claimant files suit within the applicable limitation period after the defendant dispossesses the claimant.

issues.definition: A civil possession suit is within limitation when the claimant’s possession is established, no earlier dispossession is proved, and the suit is filed within the applicable period after the defendant’s dispossession.

issues.legal_issue: A grant of property to a Hindu female gives her an absolute and alienable estate when its words and context convey full ownership, because there is no presumption that a female receives only a limited estate.
material_facts: The deceased owner made an oral will in favour of his daughter, and the women who executed the registered deed did so to carry out that will rather than to convey an estate of their own.
The deed recited that the daughter could deal with the property in any way she liked.
The daughter was the sole object of the owner’s bounty, and the circumstances showed that he intended to give her the same title he held.
The plaintiff claimed the property as an heir on the basis that the daughter had received only a limited estate; after her death, her husband mortgaged and sold the property.
issues.conclusion: The daughter became the absolute owner of the property, and her husband had full right to alienate it; the plaintiff had no title to the property. The appeal was allowed and the trial court’s dismissal of the suit was restored.
issues.legal_principle: There is no presumption that a grant of immovable property to a Hindu female is limited or inalienable, and there is no difference in this respect between a male and a female grantee. Words sufficient to convey full ownership to a male also convey full ownership to a female. The Court relied on section 8 of the Transfer of Property Act and Tagore v. Tagore, Mst. Kollani Kuar v. Luchmi Kuar, Mahomed Shumsool v. Shewukram, Nagammal v. Subbalakshmi Ammal, and Ram Gopal v. Nand Lal; it treated the principle drawn from Mahomed Shumsool as clarified by later authority and settled by Ram Gopal.

rule.if: hindu_property_grant_to_female and grant_interpretation_proceeding and grant_words_convey_full_ownership and context_shows_intention_to_grant_full_title and no_conflicting_context

predicates.hindu_property_grant_to_female: A grant of property is made to a Hindu female.
predicates.grant_interpretation_proceeding: A court is deciding the nature of the estate conveyed by a property grant.
predicates.grant_words_convey_full_ownership: The words used in the grant are sufficient to convey full ownership.
predicates.context_shows_intention_to_grant_full_ti: The surrounding circumstances show that the grantor intended to give the grantee the full title held by the grantor.
predicates.no_conflicting_context: The grant contains no conflicting context that limits the estate conveyed.

issues.definition: When a court interprets a grant of property to a Hindu female, full ownership conveyed by the grant’s words and supported by the context, without conflicting context, results in an absolute and alienable estate.
